meta.description: Tesla really said it — out loud, to a reporter, in 1896. The Evening Star of 6 June 1896 prints it as "some creation of his brain," not "the brain."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not think there is any thrill that can go through the human heart like that felt by the inventor as he sees some creation of the brain unfolding to success...Such emotions make a man forget food, sleep, friends, love, everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Tesla — spoken in an 1896 newspaper interview. We found the page: Evening Star, 6 June 1896. The printed text reads "his brain," and the "..." hides a clause.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Tesla said this out loud, to a newspaper interviewer, in the spring of 1896. It appears in a syndicated interview printed as “Chat with Tesla” in the Evening Star of Washington, D.C., 6 June 1896 ↗, and in at least three other papers that same month. One caution: every 1896 printing reads “some creation of his brain,” not “the brain,” and the familiar “…” hides a whole clause.

source.heading: The source we found

docMeta.dd: “Chat with Tesla” — Some Experiences in Handling the Electric Fluid
Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 6 June 1896, image 15 — the earliest printing we could locate in the Library of Congress newspaper archive
Unsigned in the Evening Star; the Atlanta Constitution’s 22 June 1896 reprint carries a byline printed as “Cleveland Moffitt”

source.excerpt: When I was a student I have known what it is to sit at the gaming table forty-eight hours at a stretch. I thought that an intense emotion, the fascination of play, and I believe many people regard it as the strongest emotion, but I can tell you that for many years all the allurements of the game would have seemed tame and insipid to me compared with the tremendous, overmastering excitement of my life in the laboratory. I do not think there is any thrill that can go through the human heart like that felt by the inventor as he sees some creation of his brain unfolding to success, as he watches some crucial experiment prove that through months of waiting and hoping he has been in the right. Such emotions make a man forget food, sleep, sickness, friends, love—everything.
trail: A full-text phrase search of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America newspaper archive returns exactly four matching pages, all from June 1896 ↗ — the Evening Star (6 June), the New York Sun (7 June), the Indianapolis Journal (19 June) and the Atlanta Constitution (22 June).
The earliest of the four, the Evening Star of 6 June 1896 ↗, runs the interview under the headline “Chat with Tesla” and prints the sentence inside Tesla’s own quoted speech.

The Indianapolis Journal ↗ reprints the piece as “Tesla’s Everyday Views” with the credit line “New York Sun”, while the Atlanta Constitution ↗ runs it over a byline printed as “Cleveland Moffitt” — a spelling of the American journalist Cleveland Moffett ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ still files this line under “Attributed”, citing only a 2008 secondary book. The 1896 newspaper text supplies the primary source that listing is missing.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Library of Congress scan of the Evening Star; obvious OCR slips have been corrected against the Atlanta Constitution and Indianapolis Journal printings of the same interview. Note the variant: the Evening Star and the Atlanta Constitution include “sickness” in the final list; the Indianapolis Journal’s reprint ↗ does not, and it is that shorter list which survives in the modern quotation.

author.name: Nikola Tesla
author.heading: About Nikola Tesla
author.bio: Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist and inventor, best known for his work on alternating-current power systems, induction motors and high-frequency electrical apparatus. By 1896 he was a celebrated figure in the New York press, giving late-night interviews between laboratory sessions. Because that fame long outlived him, his name is now one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for invented quotations — which makes the lines that can be tied to a dated page worth marking.

misattribution.heading: Right man, drifting words
misattribution.intro: This one is not stolen from another author — Tesla really did say it. What has gone wrong is the wording, the medium and the sourcing.

items.why: Every 1896 printing we located reads “some creation of his brain unfolding to success.” The modern circulating form says “the brain”, which flattens a personal boast into an abstraction. Compare the Evening Star scan ↗.

The “…” in the popular version stands in for a real half-sentence: “as he watches some crucial experiment prove that through months of waiting and hoping he has been in the right.” It is printed in full in the Atlanta Constitution ↗.

A Scientific American piece reproduced by Tesla Universe introduces the line with “That year he wrote” ↗. The 1896 papers present it as speech — a reporter’s transcription of Tesla talking at a café table.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the quote in its “Attributed” section, sourced to a 2008 book by Tim O’Shei rather than to anything from Tesla’s lifetime.

At least one write-up traces the quote to an “1896 New York Herald interview” ↗. The reprint it cites — the Indianapolis Journal of 19 June 1896 — carries the credit line “New York Sun” on its own page.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Tesla, spoken rather than written, and one word off: the 1896 papers say “some creation of his brain” — see the Evening Star, 6 June 1896 ↗.

context.heading: A bad night in a café
lead: The interview opens badly. The reporter finds Tesla at his usual café table around eleven at night, “looking tired and haggard,” and is told at once: “I am afraid you won’t find me a pleasant companion tonight. The fact is, I was almost killed today.” Tesla then describes taking a shock from one of his machines, a spark jumping three feet through the air to his shoulder.

The mood matters, because the famous sentence is not a boast delivered from a podium. It arrives at the low point of the talk, after Tesla has described the fire that destroyed his New York laboratory — Wikipedia dates that fire to 13 March 1895 ↗ — and admitted to spells of depression. The thrill of invention is what he offers as the thing that outweighs all of it, including, a few lines later, marriage: an inventor, he tells the reporter, should not marry.
context.detailsSummary: The four June 1896 printings, and how they differ
detailsBody: The Evening Star (6 June) headlines it “Chat with Tesla”; the New York Sun (7 June) and the Indianapolis Journal (19 June) run it as “Tesla’s Everyday Views”; the Atlanta Constitution (22 June) gives it a decorative display heading over the byline “Cleveland Moffitt.”

The only difference that touches the quoted sentence is in the final list. The Evening Star and the Atlanta Constitution print “food, sleep, sickness, friends, love”; the New York Sun and the Indianapolis Journal print “food, sleep, friends, love.” The shorter list is the one that reached the internet. Elsewhere the Sun/Indianapolis text is lightly abridged rather than merely variant — on marriage, for instance, the Evening Star has an artist “led by her love to finer achievement” where those two print “their love.”
